title: Picking a good normal example
idea: MEET. A 'normal' example is a typical input with an answer you can compute by hand. Learn to choose one that actually exercises the logic.

exercises.explanation: A normal example is a typical, everyday input — not a tricky boundary — whose answer you can work out by hand.
options: A typical input whose answer you can work out by hand
The weirdest input you can find

exercises.prompt: For 'total of a list', which is a GOOD normal example to hand-check?
exercises.explanation: [2, 3, 5] is small enough to add by hand (10) yet has several items, so it really exercises the accumulate loop.

exercises.prompt: Why is a list of 1000 numbers a POOR example to hand-check?
exercises.explanation: You can't reliably add 1000 numbers by hand, so you'd have no trustworthy answer to compare against. Keep examples hand-sized.
options: You can't work out the correct total by hand, so you can't compare

exercises.prompt: A good normal example is small enough to compute by hand but rich enough to use the logic.
exercises.explanation: Exactly — small enough to hand-check, but with enough items that the loop and any condition actually run.

exercises.prompt: For 'count scores >= 50', which normal example best exercises the condition?
exercises.explanation: [40, 70, 55] mixes failing and passing scores, so the if-condition is tested both ways — true and false.

exercises.prompt: An example where EVERY item passes the condition — what might it miss?
exercises.explanation: If every item passes, you never test the 'skip this one' path, so a bug in the reject case could hide.
options: It never tests the case where an item is skipped

exercises.prompt: Order how to build a normal example.
exercises.explanation: Pick a realistic small input, decide what a correct answer is by hand, write it down to compare later.
blocks: Work out the correct output by hand
Write down the input and its answer as your check

exercises.prompt: For 'highest bid', a good normal example puts the biggest value...
exercises.explanation: Put the max in the MIDDLE, not first or last, so you test that the loop can replace the best partway through.
options: In the middle, so the loop must update best partway through

exercises.prompt: Using the same example as the one printed in the problem is always enough.
exercises.explanation: It's a fine start, but you should add your own examples too — especially ones that stress different paths.

exercises.prompt: The real purpose of a normal example is to...
exercises.explanation: A normal example proves the common, everyday case works. Edge cases (next lessons) then cover the tricky corners.
options: Prove the everyday case works before testing tricky corners
